exercises.prompt: Read the latitude and longitude of Pine Island Light from the chart scales.
method: Draw a faint line from the light across to the side scale and read the latitude.
Draw a faint line from the light up to the top or bottom scale and read the longitude.
The light is at 33°02.3′N 149°59.9′W. Latitude comes first, longitude second.

exercises.prompt: Plot the position 33°02.6′N 150°01.4′W. Then measure the true bearing and the distance from that position to Pine Island Light.

answers.label: True bearing to Pine Island Light

method: Find the latitude on the side scale and the longitude on the top or bottom scale. Draw faint lines from each. Where they cross is the position.
Lay the parallel rule from the position to the light. Walk it to the nearest compass rose and read the true (outer) ring.
Open the dividers from the position to the light and read the distance against the latitude scale, one minute of latitude being one nautical mile.
Bearing about 103° true, distance about 1.3 nautical miles.

exercises.prompt: A vessel leaves 33°00.5′N 150°03.8′W for the Fairway Buoy. Find the true course to steer and the distance to run.
method: Plot the departure position and mark the Fairway Buoy.
Draw the track between them with the parallel rule.
Walk the rule to a compass rose and read the true course on the outer ring.
Step the dividers along the track and read the distance on the latitude scale.
Course about 034° true, distance about 3.3 nautical miles.

exercises.prompt: The true course is 034°. The compass rose gives the variation for 2020 and its yearly change. Deviation on this heading is 3° West. The year is 2026. What course do you steer by compass?
method: Update the variation: the rose says 15°00′E in 2020, decreasing 5′ a year. Six years is 30′, so variation is 14°30′E.
Go down from True to Magnetic. East is least, so subtract: true minus 14.5° gives magnetic.
Go down from Magnetic to Compass. West is best, so add the 3° West deviation.
34 − 14.5 + 3 = 22.5, so steer about 022° by compass.
assumptions: Variation in 2026 is 14°30′E (15°00′E in 2020, decreasing 5′ a year).

exercises.prompt: At 11:15 a vessel is fixed at 33°00.6′N 150°00.9′W. She steers 330° true at 6 knots with no current. Plot her dead reckoning position for 11:45.
method: Plot the fix and write the time beside it.
Draw the 330° true course line from the fix.
Distance = speed × time = 6 knots × 0.5 hour = 3.0 nautical miles.
Step off 3.0 nautical miles along the course line. Mark a dot with a half circle and write 11:45.
The DR position is about 33°03.2′N 150°02.7′W.

exercises.prompt: At the same moment a vessel takes compass bearings of Pine Island Light (034°) and Gull Rock Beacon (294°). Deviation is 3° West and the year is 2026. Find her position.
method: Update the variation to 14°30′E, as in the compass conversion exercise.
Go up from Compass to True. Compass Add East: deviation West is subtracted, then variation East is added. That is compass − 3 + 14.5 = compass + 11.5.
Pine Island Light: 34 + 11.5 ≈ 046° true. Gull Rock Beacon: 294 + 11.5 ≈ 306° true.
A bearing line is plotted from the mark, so use the reciprocal (add or subtract 180°) and draw each line back from its mark towards the vessel.
The lines cross at about 33°01.2′N 150°01.2′W. The two bearings differ by well over 30°, which gives a good fix.
assumptions: Variation in 2026 is 14°30′E. Compass bearings are rounded to the nearest degree.

exercises.prompt: The sounding at 33°01.5′N 149°59.5′W is 8.9 m. The height of tide is 1.8 m and the vessel's draught is 1.6 m. How much water is there, and what is the clearance under the keel?
method: Charted depth is measured from chart datum, so the tide is added: depth = charted depth + height of tide.
Clearance = depth − draught.
10.7 − 1.6 = 9.1 m under the keel.

exercises.prompt: Low water is at 10:00, height 0.6 m. High water is at 16:00, height 4.8 m. Use the rule of twelfths to find the height of tide at 13:00.
method: Range = 4.8 − 0.6 = 4.2 m. The tide takes six hours to rise.
Each hour the water rises 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1 twelfths of the range. 13:00 is three hours after low water.
Twelfths so far: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. That is 6/12 of the range: 4.2 × 6/12 = 2.1 m.
assumptions: The rule of twelfths is an approximation that assumes a regular six-hour tide. These tide figures are invented for the exercise.

exercises.prompt: Sentinel Rock dries 1.2 m. A vessel drawing 1.5 m wants at least 0.5 m of water under her keel when she passes over the rock. Low water is at 10:00, height 0.6 m. High water is at 16:00, height 4.8 m. What height of tide is needed, and at what time on the rising tide is it first reached?

answers.label: Earliest time, as minutes after midnight on the 24-hour clock

method: A drying height is measured above chart datum, so water over the rock = height of tide − drying height.
The water over the rock must cover the draught plus the margin: 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 m.
Tide needed = 1.2 + 2.0 = 3.2 m.
Work out the tide hour by hour from the rule of twelfths: 10:00 0.6 m, 11:00 0.95 m, 12:00 1.65 m, 13:00 2.7 m, 14:00 3.75 m.
3.2 m falls between 13:00 and 14:00. It is reached about 29 minutes after 13:00, so about 13:29.
assumptions: Tide figures are invented for the exercise. Treat the rise within each hour as steady.
